title: Ang 696–705: Jaitsri
tomorrow: what does a ballad for heroes sound like when it's sung to God?

lines: THE ONE WHO DEALS WITH THE SPIDER.
FEAR HAS COME INTO MY HEART.
cards: Friend groups tend to have one: the one who deals with the spider, drives in the snow, makes the awkward phone call. So what happens when that person says, quietly, I'm scared?
Jaitsri opens on ang 696 with Guru Ram Das: the jewel of the Name lives in my heart; the Guru placed his hand on my forehead.
A few pages on, a hymn by Guru Tegh Bahadur, whom Sikhs remember for giving his life so others could keep their faith, says it out loud. Fear has come into my heart.

teach.h: SAVE MY HONOR. FEAR HAS COME IN.
teach.b: In paraphrase: Lord, save my honor. Fear of death has come into my heart; I've taken hold of your shelter, ocean of mercy. Sikhs read a line like this in two ways, and each has a strong case.
The first: the Guru is speaking in the seeker's voice. Gurbani often does this, taking on the voice of the one who struggles, the way the Gurus sing as a bride waiting for her husband.
Its best case: the hymn hands you words for your own worst night. The fear is yours; the Guru gives it a shape and a direction.
The second: these are the Guru's own words, meant plainly.

teach.h: BOTH TAKE THE FEAR TO SHELTER.
teach.b: Its best case: this is the Guru Sikhs remember for courage, and here he writes that fear came in, and that he held on. Then strength isn't the absence of fear. It's where you take it.
The two readings disagree about whose fear it is. They agree on where it goes: into the shelter. And both meet the raga's first page, a hand placed on the forehead.
Not a shout, not armor. Someone bowing their head to be held.

how: Jaitsri is one of the ragas of the Guru Granth Sahib, and its hymns, including Guru Tegh Bahadur's 'save my honor', are sung in kirtan; Sikh readers discuss whether such pleas voice the seeker or the Guru himself.

s: a hymn by a Guru remembered for courage would never mention fear
Guru Tegh Bahadur's Jaitsri hymn says fear has come into the heart, and takes God's shelter.
Jaitsri opens with the picture of the Guru's hand on the forehead
Guru Ram Das: the jewel of the Name lives in my heart; the Guru placed his hand on my forehead.
Sikhs all read 'save my honor' in exactly the same way
some hear the seeker's voice, given to us; others hear the Guru's own words, meant plainly.

games.q: at dinner your uncle says the 'save my honor' hymn is the Guru speaking for us. your aunt says it's his own honest fear. your little cousin asks who's right. what fits?
o: Sikhs hold both readings, and both end with the fear taken to shelter.
your uncle: a Guru would never really write about being afraid.
your aunt: and that means the stories of his courage are overstated.
games.why: the two readings disagree about whose fear it is, and agree on where it goes. neither says courage means feeling nothing.

practice: Rest one hand lightly on your forehead, the way the hymn on ang 696 pictures the Guru's hand. Let your head be a little heavy in your palm, and breathe.
Whatever is worrying you can sit there too; the hand doesn't push it away, it just holds.
